article.title: The Grid Bottleneck Behind the AI Data-Centre Boom
article.author: OpenAI
article.why: AI 擴張也受電網限制。

paragraphs.en:
The AI boom is often described as a race for chips, models, and data centres. Yet another limit may shape how fast new computing capacity can grow: the power grid. A data centre can be planned and built faster than a large power connection. Grid studies, permits, substations, transformers, transmission work, and utility agreements can take years. As a result, servers may be ready before the electricity system is ready to serve them.

AI sites create a special problem because they place very large demand in one location. A server campus may need hundreds of megawatts. Utilities must check whether local generation, wires, transformers, and substations can carry that load while keeping service reliable for other users. If the network is too weak, new equipment must be built before the site can open.

Connection queues make the timing harder to predict. Power plants, batteries, factories, and data centres may all seek access to the same grid. Each request can need an engineering study. If an earlier project changes size or leaves the queue, later studies may need to be updated. So a queue is not only a list of projects waiting their turn. It is also a process for testing how each project changes the network.

This constraint affects location choices. In the past, operators often focused on land cost, tax support, fibre links, and distance to customers. Those factors still matter, but access to firm power is becoming just as important. A region with higher electricity prices may be more attractive if it can provide a connection years earlier. In that case, time to power can matter as much as the price of power.

Energy and capacity are also different. A region may produce enough electricity over a full year but still be unable to deliver enough power to one site at a certain hour. Wind and solar can add low-carbon energy, but they do not automatically solve local grid limits or periods of low output. Storage, flexible demand, gas, nuclear power, and stronger links between regions can all help, depending on local conditions.

For technology companies, the grid creates execution risk. A project may have chips, buildings, and customers but still miss its launch date because a substation is late. A long-term power contract may also depend on transmission work that is not complete. Investors should therefore ask how much power is requested, studied, contracted, permitted, financed, energized, and physically deliverable. An announced number is not the same as usable capacity.

Power limits can also change AI operations. Training jobs are often more flexible about location and time than consumer services that need very low latency. Some work can move to sites or hours with more power. Companies can also raise server utilization, improve cooling, schedule jobs better, and use more efficient models. When new grid capacity is hard to obtain, each megawatt becomes more valuable.

Public policy faces trade-offs as well. Data centres can bring jobs, investment, and tax revenue, but grid upgrades can be costly. Regulators must decide how those costs are shared and how to protect other customers. At the same time, approval that is too slow can delay useful infrastructure. Faster planning therefore has to be balanced with reliability, transparency, and environmental review.

The main lesson is that AI infrastructure is a system, not a pile of servers. Chips, buildings, networks, power, cooling, finance, and permits must arrive in the right order. Improving only one part can move the bottleneck somewhere else. Managers should treat electricity as part of the technology roadmap from the start. They should also plan with stages rather than headlines: requested capacity, studied capacity, contracted capacity, energized capacity, and operating capacity. Those gaps show where schedule risk really sits.

Efficiency is one way to respond while a grid connection is fixed. Better hardware use, cooling, workload timing, and model design can increase useful computing without adding another megawatt. In a power-constrained market, efficiency is therefore not only an environmental goal. It is also a way to turn limited infrastructure into more usable AI capacity.

This perspective changes due diligence. The key question is not how much capacity is announced, but how much can actually receive power on the planned date.
paragraphs.zh: AI 基礎設施不只受晶片限制，也受電網限制。大型供電連接常需多年研究、許可、變電站與輸電工程，而 AI 園區又把數百 MW 需求集中在小區域。Connection queue 包含工程研究，因此 power availability 與 time to power 會影響選址。全年 energy 足夠，不代表特定時間與地點有足夠 capacity；再生能源、儲能、彈性需求與其他電源仍需和輸電配合。公司即使已有晶片與建築，也可能因供電工程延誤而無法上線，所以應區分 requested、studied、contracted、permitted、energized 與 operational capacity。Grid constraint 也提高 workload 移轉、利用率、冷卻、排程與 model efficiency 的價值。電力應從一開始就納入 technology roadmap。
paragraphs.ja: AIインフラはチップだけでなく電力にも制約されます。大規模接続には系統調査、許認可、変電所、送電工事で年単位の時間がかかり、AI施設は狭い地域へ数百MW級の需要を集中させます。接続キューも技術調査を含むため、power availability と time to power が立地を左右します。年間energyが十分でも特定時刻・地点のcapacityが足りるとは限りません。企業はチップと建物があっても電力工事の遅れで稼働できないため、requested、studied、contracted、permitted、energized、operational capacity を分けて確認します。系統制約は負荷移動、利用率、冷却、スケジューリング、model efficiency の価値を高めます。電力は最初から technology roadmap に入れるべきです。
